message.content: Lions (family Felidae) and zebras (family Equidae) share a very distant common ancestor that lived roughly 70–80 million years ago during the late Paleocene/early Eocene. At that time the lineage that would become the modern carnivores (Carnivora) was splitting off from the lineage that would become the odd‑toed ungulates (Perissodactyla). Thus the last common ancestor of lions and zebras was a small, likely insectivorous or omnivorous mammal that belonged to the broader clade Laurasiatheria, the group that contains all modern placental mammals descended from the early “Laurasiatherian” radiation.
message.reasoning:
The user asks: "What is the common ancestor of lion and zebra?" They want an answer. We can provide a general evolutionary biology answer: The most recent common ancestor (MRCA) of lions (Panthera leo) and zebras (Equus quagga) would be a common ancestor of the family Felidae (cats) and Equidae (horses). But lions belong to order Carnivora, suborder Feliformia; zebras belong to order Perissodactyla. Their MRCA would be at the level of the clade that includes all mammals? Actually, the last common ancestor of cats and horses would be at the level of the clade that includes all placental mammals? Let's think: Lions are within the clade Carnivora, which is part of Laurasiatheria. Zebras are within Perissodactyla, also part of Laurasiatheria. So their MRCA would be within Laurasiatheria, perhaps the clade that includes all Laurasiatherian mammals. That might be the last common ancestor of the superorders Laurasiatheria. But we could say: The last common ancestor of lions and zebras lived around 70 million years ago, when the ancestors of the two lineages diverged from other Laurasiatherians. So the answer: The common ancestor would be a small mammal-like creature that gave rise to both the carnivore lineage leading to lions and the perissodactyl lineage leading to zebras. It would have been a small, probably insectivorous or omnivorous mammal living in the Paleocene/Eocene.

We should give a concise answer. No tool needed.
